title: NRI Property Sales in India: TDS Rules Every Buyer Must Get Right
excerpt: TDS on a property bought from an NRI is 12.5% of the full sale price — not 1% — and from October 1 the buyer's TAN requirement is gone. Here is the compliance checklist.
body:
• From October 1, a resident individual or HUF buying immovable property from an NRI no longer needs a TAN. The buyer uses their PAN and deposits the deducted TDS through Form 141, which has a new Schedule E for such transactions.
  • When the seller is a resident, TDS is 1% on properties valued at ₹50 lakh or more. When the seller is an NRI, TDS applies from the first rupee at 12.5% plus surcharge and 4% health-and-education cess — deducted on the entire sale consideration, not just the capital gain.
  • NRI sellers facing withholding far above their actual tax liability can apply for a lower or nil deduction certificate (Form 13) before the sale is finalized, so the buyer deducts at the certified rate. TDS must be deposited within 30 days from the end of the deduction month, and a Form 132 certificate issued to the seller.
  • Buyer beware: verify the seller's residential status before paying. Deducting only 1% on an NRI purchase leaves a shortfall that the tax department treats as default — 1% monthly interest on the shortfall, and in extreme cases a penalty equal to the shortfall itself.

One administrative headache removed

Buying a house from a non-resident Indian has always carried more tax paperwork than buying from a resident — and one part of that process just got simpler. A resident individual or Hindu undivided family (HUF) buying immovable property from an NRI no longer needs a Tax Deduction and Collection Account Number (TAN) just to deduct tax at source on the transaction. Instead, the buyer can use their PAN and deposit the TDS through Form 141, now expanded with a new Schedule E specifically for NRI-seller transactions.

The 1% versus 12.5% two-track system

The headline difference is the rate. When the seller is a resident, the buyer deducts 1% — and only when the consideration is ₹50 lakh or more. When the seller is an NRI, TDS applies from the first rupee, with no minimum threshold, at 12.5% plus surcharge and cess: the same rate as long-term capital gains tax.

The rate also depends on holding period. Property held over 24 months attracts the 12.5% long-term rate; property sold within 24 months is short-term capital gain taxed at the seller's slab rate, where buyers commonly deduct around 30%. And because the buyer cannot know the seller's actual gain, withholding is applied on the entire sale consideration. On a ₹2 crore sale, that can mean ₹25 lakh withheld even if the seller's real gain is far smaller.

The buyer's burden — and the costly 1% mistake

The critical point is that the responsibility to deduct the correct TDS rests entirely with the buyer. Before making any payment, the buyer should establish the seller's residential status: deducting only 1% on an NRI purchase leaves a large shortfall, and the tax department can treat the buyer as an assessee in default. Interest of 1% per month runs on the shortfall until it is actually deducted and paid; in extreme cases — typically where the NRI seller did not pay the remaining tax and scrutiny is opened — the assessing officer can impose a penalty equal to the shortfall.

Under the new process, the buyer files Schedule E of Form 141 — property address, sale consideration, stamp duty value, payment date, buyer-seller details, plus the NRI's overseas address, residential status and PAN — deposits the TDS within 30 days from the end of the deduction month, and issues a TDS certificate in Form 132 to the seller.

What NRI sellers can do about excess withholding

The relief valve is the lower or nil deduction certificate. An NRI seller whose real tax liability is far below 12.5% of the sale price — because the gain is small relative to the price, or exemptions apply — can obtain the certificate through Form 13 before the sale is finalized, and the buyer then deducts at the certified rate. This keeps money from being locked up for months awaiting a refund.

NRIs can also cut the final liability by reinvesting gains under Sections 54, 54F and 54EC — another Indian residential property or specified capital-gains bonds. On the money trail, proceeds are typically credited to an NRO account first; repatriating them abroad requires Forms 15CA and 15CB with bank documentation and CA certification, and banks routinely verify TDS compliance before allowing outward remittance.

What to watch

The October 1 change removes a 2-to-10-day TAN allotment delay from NRI property deals — a genuine simplification. But it does nothing to dilute the buyer's compliance risk. The practical checklist: establish residential status first, get the Form 13 certificate before closing if withholding will exceed the real liability, deposit on time, and keep the Form 132 paper trail — because the department will.
